title: The Man Born Blind Receives His Sight
summary: Jesus heals a man blind from birth by putting mud on his eyes and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath, the Pharisees interrogate the man and his frightened parents, and when the man insists that Jesus must be from God, they throw him out. Jesus finds him, the man believes and worships, and Jesus declares that he came so the blind may see and those who claim to see may become blind.
story:
Jesus has just said, “I am the light of the world” (8:12), and in 9:5 he says it again before showing what it means. The chapter stands as a picture of the whole Gospel in miniature. A man who has never seen moves step by step toward faith, calling Jesus a man, then a prophet, then one from God, and finally Lord, whom he worships. Meanwhile the religious authorities, who are sure they see, move step by step into deeper blindness. It also shows the cost of confessing Jesus, as the man loses his place in the synagogue, which prepares for Jesus' teaching about the good shepherd in chapter 10.

The chapter continues the conflict of chapters 5 to 8. Like the healing at Bethesda (chapter 5), this sign is done on a Sabbath, to a man who did not ask for it, and it leads to an investigation of the healer rather than joy at the healing. Chapter 8 ended with Jesus' claim before Abraham and an attempt to stone him (8:58-59). Chapter 9 moves the argument from Jesus to someone who has met him: the authorities cannot reach Jesus, so they put his first witness on trial. The verdict they reach, that the man is to be thrown out, and the verdict Jesus pronounces at the end, that those who claim to see remain in their guilt (9:41), run straight into the shepherd discourse, which is spoken to the same Pharisees (10:6, 10:19-21).
historical:
The chapter is most likely still set in the autumn season of the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 7:37), before the winter Feast of Dedication in 10:22. That matters for its imagery. The Mishnah remembers that during Tabernacles great golden lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, so bright that every courtyard in Jerusalem reflected their light (m. Sukkah 5:2-3), and that each morning a priest filled a golden flagon at the Pool of Siloam and poured the water at the altar (m. Sukkah 4:9). Jesus' claims to be the light of the world (8:12, 9:5) and his sending a blind man to Siloam both stand against that background.

The Pool of Siloam lay at the southern end of the old City of David, fed by the Gihon spring through the tunnel cut in King Hezekiah's day, around 700 BC (2 Kings 20:20, 2 Chronicles 32:30). The Hebrew inscription carved by the tunnel's diggers was found in 1880. Isaiah already speaks of the gently flowing waters of Shiloah (Isaiah 8:6). In 2004, during work on a sewer line, the steps of a large stepped pool of the Second Temple period came to light just south of the smaller pool that later pilgrims were shown; Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron excavated it, and it was announced in 2005. Most archaeologists identify it with the pool of Jesus' day, a public pool large enough for crowds of pilgrims, probably used for ritual immersion. As with Bethesda in chapter 5, John's knowledge of Jerusalem's water system fits what excavation has found.

Verse 22 says the Jews had already agreed that anyone confessing Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. The Jews here must be the authorities, since the parents who fear them are Jews too. J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968) argued that John was telling two stories at once, one about Jesus and one about his own community decades later, and he linked the verse to the Birkat ha-Minim, the benediction against heretics that the Babylonian Talmud says Samuel the Small composed at Yavneh under Rabban Gamaliel (b. Berakhot 28b-29a), usually dated to the 80s AD. Reuven Kimelman (in Jewish and Christian Self-Definition, volume 2, 1981) and others have since shown that the benediction's date, wording, and target are uncertain and that it was not originally aimed at Christians as such, and Jonathan Bernier (Aposynagōgos and the Historical Jesus in John, 2013) argued that local exclusions of Jesus' followers are plausible during his own ministry. Exclusion from a community was an old practice: Ezra 10:8 threatens separation from the assembly of the exiles, and the Qumran Community Rule sets out graded penalties of exclusion from the fellowship of the members (1QS 6:24-7:25). Whichever setting is right, the chapter reflects a real and painful separation, and it describes the leaders' action, not the character of the Jewish people. Reading it as the latter has fed Christian hostility toward Jews for centuries, and the text does not support it: the man, his parents, the neighbors, and the divided Pharisees of verse 16 are all Jews.
cultural:
Many in the ancient world assumed that disability was punishment for sin. The disciples' question reflects a real debate. The Babylonian Talmud records Rabbi Ammi's principle that there is no death without sin and no suffering without iniquity, and then records the rabbis refuting it (b. Shabbat 55a-b). If the man was born blind, could he have sinned before birth? A midrash on Genesis 25:22 pictures Esau struggling to get out of Rebekah's womb whenever she passed a temple of idols (Genesis Rabbah 63:6), so the idea of prenatal sin was thinkable. The Old Testament speaks of consequences reaching to children (Exodus 20:5), but it also rejects the idea that children bear their parents' guilt (Ezekiel 18:20), and the book of Job argues at length against the claim that suffering always reveals sin. Jesus makes the same refusal in Luke 13:1-5.

A man blind from birth had almost no way to earn a living except begging, often near the temple gates or on the roads into the city (compare Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46 and the lame man at the Beautiful Gate in Acts 3:2). The Talmud lists the blind among four kinds of people who are counted as though dead, with the poor, the leper, and the childless (b. Nedarim 64b). That is why his neighbors know him only as the man who sat and begged (verse 8), and why they are not sure the man who can now see is the same person.

Saliva was widely thought to have healing power. Jesus uses it elsewhere (Mark 7:33, 8:23), and the Roman historian Tacitus reports that the emperor Vespasian, at Alexandria in AD 69 or 70, was asked by a blind man to anoint his eyes with spittle (Histories 4.81). Making mud, however, involved kneading, which the Mishnah lists among the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (m. Shabbat 7:2), and the Jerusalem Talmud records a ruling against putting even fasting spittle on the eyes as a remedy on the Sabbath (y. Shabbat 14:4). The rabbis allowed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath (m. Yoma 8:6), but a lifelong blindness was no emergency. The healing could have waited a day, and Jesus did not wait.

The parents' answer that their son is of age (hēlikia, verse 21) means that he is an adult who can give legal testimony for himself; the Mishnah puts the age for keeping the commandments at thirteen (m. Avot 5:21). When the authorities tell the man, “Give glory to God!” (verse 24), they use the formula Joshua spoke to Achan (Joshua 7:19), a solemn summons to tell the truth and confess; the Mishnah uses the same text for the confession of a condemned man (m. Sanhedrin 6:2). Their claim to be disciples of Moses (verse 28) sets two teachers against each other. Being put out of the synagogue meant losing one's standing in the local community: its worship, its fellowship, marriage prospects, and often practical support.
literary:
The chapter is one of John's finest pieces of drama, built in scenes like a play: the healing (verses 1 to 7), the neighbors (8 to 12), the first interrogation (13 to 17), the parents (18 to 23), the second interrogation (24 to 34), and Jesus with the man and then with the Pharisees (35 to 41). Jesus is present only at the beginning and end; in between, the man stands alone. Many readers see the scenes arranged around the parents' fearful testimony at the center, with the healing and the final revelation at either end, and the two interrogations balancing each other.

The irony is thick. The man who was blind grows in sight and in courage. He calls his healer “The man they call Jesus” (verse 11), then says “He is a prophet” (verse 17), then argues that he must be from God (verse 33), and at last says, “Lord, I believe” (verse 38). The authorities move the other way, from division (verse 16) to disbelief (verse 18) to insult (verse 34). Knowledge claims drive the dialogue: the parents say what they know and do not know (verses 20 to 21), the authorities say “We know” twice (verses 24 and 29), and the man answers with the one thing he knows (verse 25) and then with “We know” of his own (verse 31). He also answers with wit, asking whether they want to become Jesus' disciples too (verse 27). The words for seeing and for blindness recur throughout, so that by the last verses physical sight has become a picture of spiritual sight.

Small details carry weight. When his neighbors argue over who he is, the man says ‘I am’ (egō eimi, verse 9), the very words Jesus uses of himself throughout the Gospel; here they mean only ‘It is I’, but John's readers hear the echo. John translates Siloam as “Sent” (verse 7), a quiet pointer to Jesus, whom the Gospel calls the one sent by the Father again and again (3:17, 5:36, 7:29, 8:42, 17:3). Martyn's reading of the chapter as a two-level drama, in which the man's trial also mirrors the trials of later believers, has shaped modern study, whatever one concludes about its dating.

outline.t: Jesus heals a man born blind
The Pharisees question him: a prophet
The second interrogation and the man thrown out
Jesus finds him; sight and blindness

doctrines.note: Jesus refuses the disciples' assumption that this suffering must be traced to a particular sin (verse 3). He turns the question from why to what God will do. The chapter doesn't explain all suffering, but it closes off the easy link between a person's pain and their guilt, and it shows the works of God displayed in a life that others had written off.

The healing is done on a Sabbath by an act the rabbis counted as work (verse 14), and it splits the Pharisees: some say a Sabbath-breaker cannot be from God, others that a sinner could not do such signs (verse 16). As in 5:17, Jesus acts as one who shares his Father's work, which does not stop on the Sabbath.

Faith grows through the chapter as testimony under pressure. The man begins with what he knows, “I was blind, but now I see!” (verse 25), and comes to full confession only when Jesus reveals himself: “Lord, I believe” (verse 38).

The chapter ends with the man bowing before Jesus (verse 38), the verb John used for worship of the Father in 4:20-24. The one expelled from the synagogue's worship finds the one to whom worship belongs.

Jesus says, “For judgment I have come into this world” (verse 39). His coming exposes people. Those who admit their blindness receive sight, while those who claim to see without him are confirmed in their blindness and their guilt remains (verse 41).

words.note: Tuphlos, blind. It occurs about fifty times in the New Testament and sixteen times in John, thirteen of them in this chapter. It begins as a physical description (verse 1) and ends as a spiritual diagnosis when the Pharisees ask, “Are we blind too?” (verse 40). Isaiah had promised that the eyes of the blind would be opened in the day of God's salvation (Isaiah 35:5) and that the Lord's servant would open blind eyes (Isaiah 42:7), which gives the healing a messianic weight.

Pēlos, clay or mud. It occurs six times in the New Testament, five in this chapter and once in Romans 9:21, where it is the potter's clay. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the clay in the potter's hand (Isaiah 29:16, Jeremiah 18:6). The repeated mention of the mud keeps the Sabbath offense in view, and it invited early readers such as Irenaeus to see the Creator at work shaping a man from the ground.

Silōam, Siloam. It occurs three times in the New Testament: here (verses 7 and 11) and in Luke 13:4, where a tower near Siloam fell and killed eighteen people. The name renders the Hebrew Shiloah (Isaiah 8:6), from the verb shalach, to send, probably because the water was sent through the channel from the spring. John translates it as “Sent” (verse 7), linking the water that heals to Jesus, whom the Gospel repeatedly calls the one sent by the Father.

Hamartōlos, sinner or sinful. It occurs about forty-seven times in the New Testament, most often in Luke, but in John only in this chapter (verses 16, 24, 25, and 31). In Jewish usage it could mean a person who openly disregarded the law. The whole trial turns on whether Jesus is a sinner because he broke the Sabbath, and the man's refusal to call him one (verse 25) is the hinge of his testimony.

Homologeō, to confess or declare openly. It occurs about twenty-six times in the New Testament and four times in John: of the Baptist, who confessed that he was not the Christ (1:20), here (verse 22), and of the rulers who believed but would not confess for fear of being put out (12:42). To confess Jesus is a public act with public consequences.

Aposunagōgos, put out of the synagogue. The word appears only in John (9:22, 12:42, 16:2) and is not found in any earlier surviving Greek text. It names exclusion from the local Jewish community, the price the man pays for his testimony, and Jesus warns his disciples of the same in 16:2. BDAG glosses it as expelled from the synagogue, and its exact legal form in the first century is debated.

Proskuneō, to worship, originally to bow down before someone. It occurs about sixty times in the New Testament and eleven times in John, nine of them in the conversation about worship with the Samaritan woman (4:20-24), where it is directed to the Father. It can mean respectful homage to a human superior, but its use here, after the man's confession of faith, is the climax of his growing sight.

Krima, judgment or verdict. It occurs about twenty-seven times in the New Testament and only here in John, which usually uses krisis. In verse 39 it names the result of Jesus' coming rather than the act of condemning: his presence sorts people by how they respond to the light. John holds this together with 3:17, where the Son was not sent to condemn the world; judgment is the shadow cast by a light that people refuse.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the light of the world in action. The prophets promised that in the day of God's salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 29:18, 35:5), that the Lord's servant would be a light for the nations and would open blind eyes (Isaiah 42:6-7), and Psalm 146:8 says it is the Lord who opens the eyes of the blind. The Old Testament records no healing of a man born blind; even Tobit, in the book that bears his name, had seen before he lost his sight (Tobit 2:10, 11:10-13). So the man is right to say that no one had ever heard of such a thing (verse 32), and his argument that only one from God could do it points further than he knows.

Many interpreters since Irenaeus have also seen a sign of new creation here, reading the mud from the ground as a thematic echo of God forming the first man from the dust (Genesis 2:7). The text doesn't draw the link itself, but it does show Jesus giving sight to one who never had it, a work of making rather than repair. The man is sent to wash in the pool called Sent, and the one who sends him is the Sent One of the Father.

The chapter also shows Jesus as the shepherd who seeks out the one thrown out. When the man is expelled, Jesus finds him (verse 35), as the Lord promised in Ezekiel 34:16 to seek the lost and bring back the strays; chapter 10 will make that promise explicit. Jesus reveals himself as the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7:13-14 to whom dominion and judgment are given (compare John 5:27), and he receives the man's worship. At the end he speaks as that judge (verse 39), and his verdict falls not on the man the leaders called born in sin but on the leaders who claimed to see.
interpretation:
Early Christian readers found in this chapter both a sign of the Creator and a picture of baptism. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 5.15.2, around 180) argued that when Jesus made clay and anointed the man's eyes he showed that he was the same Word whose hand had formed Adam from the earth, supplying in public what had been left unformed in the womb. Justin Martyr (First Apology 61, around 155) calls baptism illumination, and the name stuck: the newly baptized were ‘the enlightened’. Healings of the blind appear among the scenes painted in the Roman catacombs. Augustine (Tractates on John 44, early fifth century) read the blind man as the human race, blind from its first parent; the spittle mixed with earth as the Word made flesh; the anointing as the making of a catechumen; and the washing in Siloam, the pool of the Sent One, as baptism into Christ.

That reading shaped the church's calendar. In the ancient Roman practice of preparing adults for baptism at Easter, John 4, 9, and 11 were read on Sundays in Lent, and the modern Roman Catholic rite for adult initiation and the Revised Common Lectionary both keep John 9 on the fourth Sunday of Lent in Year A, the Sunday of the second scrutiny. In the Orthodox churches the sixth Sunday after Pascha is the Sunday of the Blind Man. Medieval readers followed Augustine; Thomas Aquinas's Lectures on John (around 1270) gather the patristic readings, and the Glossa Ordinaria carried them into the schools. Calvin's commentary (1553) stressed verse 3: God has reasons for afflictions that are hidden from us, and we are not to judge a sufferer's guilt by his suffering.

In art, Duccio's panel of the healing, painted for the predella of the Maestà in Siena Cathedral (1308 to 1311) and now in the National Gallery, London, shows the man twice, receiving the touch and then washing, and El Greco painted the healing of the blind three times in his Italian years (Dresden, the Metropolitan Museum, and Parma, about 1567 to 1573). John Newton's hymn Amazing Grace, written for New Year's Day 1773 and published in the Olney Hymns (1779), borrows the man's confession in verse 25 for its first stanza.

Modern scholarship has concentrated on the expulsion. Martyn's two-level reading (1968) and Raymond Brown's The Community of the Beloved Disciple (1979) made John 9 the main window onto the history of a Johannine community in conflict with a synagogue. Kimelman (1981), Adele Reinhartz (Befriending the Beloved Disciple, 2001), and Bernier (2013) have questioned that reconstruction from different sides. Jewish readers have pressed Christians to hear how the Jews of this chapter have been used against real Jewish neighbors. Readers with disabilities, and scholars writing from that experience, have also asked whether the chapter treats blindness only as a metaphor for sin; the text's own answer in verse 3 is that it does not.
text:
Several manuscript differences show up between English Bibles in this chapter. In verse 4 the earliest manuscripts and the modern critical editions read ‘we must work the works’, so the disciples are included; later manuscripts and the King James Version read ‘I must work’. A smaller group of early witnesses also reads ‘the works of him who sent us’, but most keep ‘sent Me’. The shift to ‘I’ is easy to explain as a scribe's smoothing, which is why modern versions keep ‘we’.

In verse 35 Jesus asks, in the oldest manuscripts, including the papyri P66 and P75 and the codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and Washingtonianus, whether the man believes in the Son of Man. Later manuscripts and the King James Version read ‘the Son of God’. Because scribes were far more likely to change the unusual question to the familiar confession than the reverse, modern versions read Son of Man.

Verses 38 and the first words of 39 (“Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus. Then Jesus declared) are missing from P75, the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Washingtonianus, and a few Old Latin and Coptic witnesses. Calvin L. Porter (New Testament Studies 13, 1967) argued that the words were a liturgical addition from the church's use of the chapter in baptismal instruction, and some scholars agree; others think the omission was an accident, since the surrounding sentences begin alike. All major English versions print the words, some with a note.

Some differences are only translation. In verse 24 the King James Version reads ‘Give God the praise’, where modern versions have ‘Give glory to God’; the Greek is the formula of Joshua 7:19. In verse 7 older versions keep the transliteration Siloam but also give its meaning, as the Greek does.

teach.big: Jesus, the light of the world, gives sight to a man everyone had written off, and the same light exposes those who are sure they already see.

outline.t: Jesus refuses to treat suffering as a puzzle about who is to blame and turns it into an occasion for the works of God, which he does while it is day.
The healing is a new-creation act, and the man's obedience to a strange command comes before he can see anything.
A changed life raises questions others cannot answer, and the man starts with plain testimony about what happened.
Religious experts divide over rules and signs, and the man, pressed for a verdict, moves from ‘a man’ to ‘a prophet’.
The parents show how fear of exclusion silences honest witness, even when the facts are not in dispute.
One thing I know: the man holds to his experience, reasons from Scripture's pattern, and pays for it with his place in the community.
Jesus seeks out the one who has been thrown out, reveals himself as the Son of Man, and is worshiped.
Judgment falls on the claim to see: admitted blindness can be healed, but self-assured blindness keeps its guilt.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading uses verse 3 to say that God inflicts disability in order to show off a miracle, as if the man's decades of darkness were only a stage set. Jesus is answering the disciples' question about blame, and he turns from cause to purpose; the text does not say God made the man blind for show, and teachers should not say it either. The opposite misreading drops verse 3 altogether and treats the blind man as a mere symbol, when John tells his story with concrete names, places, and a family.

A second pitfall is to preach the man as a model of heroic courage while treating his parents as villains. Their fear is understandable, and John reports it without contempt; the point is what fear does to testimony, a pressure every listener knows. A third is to make the Jews or the Pharisees of this chapter a picture of Jewish people generally. Jesus, the man, his parents, and the Pharisees who defend him (verse 16) are all Jews; the target of verses 39 to 41 is anyone who claims to see without Jesus, which includes religious people in churches. A fourth is to treat blindness in verses 39 to 41 as a simple insult. Jesus' verdict is that admitting one's blindness is the beginning of sight, which makes the passage an invitation as much as a rebuke.

Finally, avoid turning verse 4 into a general call to busyness. The night that is coming is first of all the hour of Jesus' death, and the we of the verse draws the disciples into his mission, not into anxious activity.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people with disabilities and their families, who have often heard some version of the disciples' question from Christians: what did you, or your parents, do to deserve this? Teach verse 3 as Jesus' refusal of that question, and do not imply that every disability is waiting to be cured or that a lack of healing reflects weak faith. It also presses on anyone who has been expelled or shunned by a religious community, sometimes for telling the truth. The man thrown out is the one Jesus goes looking for. Parents in the room who kept silent when a child needed their support may feel the sting of verses 20 to 23; the story names their fear without mocking it, and there is room to speak of repair. Where people have been harmed by religious leaders who used their authority to silence questions, the passage can be taught as Jesus' judgment on that abuse, but not in a way that invites the room to despise all authority or to exempt itself from the warning in verse 41.

hard.q: Was the man born blind just so that God could display his power in him?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. Read quickly, verse 3 sounds as if God made the man suffer for decades as the setting for a miracle. Philosophers who press the problem of evil, from David Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) onward, have asked what kind of goodness would allow gratuitous suffering in order to be praised for relieving it, and on this reading the verse seems to make the point for them. The disciples' own assumption, that suffering tracks sin, has a long history too: the Talmud records Rabbi Ammi's principle that there is no suffering without iniquity, though the same passage goes on to refute it (b. Shabbat 55a-b).

Interpreters answer in several ways. Some note that the oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the sentence can end with ‘neither this man nor his parents sinned’, and the purpose clause can join the following verse: so that the works of God may be displayed in him, we must work while it is day. On that reading Jesus is not explaining why the blindness happened but saying what he will do about it. Others keep the traditional punctuation, as most translations do, and read it as a statement that God's purpose reaches into this man's life without claiming that God inflicted the blindness for show; Calvin's commentary takes this line, saying God has reasons we cannot see and we must not judge a sufferer's guilt by his suffering. Still others stress that Jesus is primarily rejecting the disciples' theory of sin and blame rather than offering a full account of why suffering exists, much as he does in Luke 13:1-5.

All these readings agree that Jesus refuses to treat suffering as a puzzle about guilt, and that his response to it is to act. The chapter does not give a complete answer to why God allows suffering. What it shows is a God who does not stand at a distance from it, and a Savior who stops for a beggar no one else stopped for.

hard.q: Does this chapter describe what happened in Jesus' lifetime, or conflicts between church and synagogue decades later, and is it anti-Jewish?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the critical case was made by J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968). He argued that a formal decision to expel anyone who confessed Jesus as Messiah (verse 22) did not exist in Jesus' lifetime, that it matches the Birkat ha-Minim of the late first century, and that John has projected the experience of his own community back into Jesus' ministry. Raymond Brown (The Community of the Beloved Disciple, 1979) built on this. Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018) have added that, whatever its origin, the chapter's portrait of the Jews as persecutors has been used for centuries to justify Christian contempt for Jews, and that readers must face that history honestly.

The responses come from two directions. On the history, Reuven Kimelman (1981) and others have shown that the Birkat ha-Minim cannot be securely dated to John's time or shown to have targeted Christians, which removes the main support for Martyn's dating, and Jonathan Bernier (Aposynagōgos and the Historical Jesus in John, 2013) argued that local synagogue exclusions of Jesus' followers are historically plausible within his lifetime, since Jewish communities already practiced forms of exclusion (Ezra 10:8, 1QS 6:24-7:25). Many scholars take a middle course: the event is told with an eye on later readers who faced the same pressure, as the two-level reading suggests, without being invented. On the question of anti-Judaism, interpreters from many traditions point out that everyone in the chapter is Jewish, including the healed man and the Pharisees who defend Jesus (verse 16); that the phrase the Jews in verse 22 must mean a group of leaders, since the parents who fear them are Jews; and that the chapter's verdict falls on the claim to see, which John addresses to every reader. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture's truthfulness are found on both sides of the dating question, and all can agree that the text gives no warrant for hostility toward Jewish people.

observe: Trace what the man says about Jesus in verses 11, 17, 25, 33, and 38. How does his description change?
What reasons do the Pharisees give in verse 16 for opposite conclusions about Jesus?
What exactly do the parents say they know and do not know, and why does John say they answered that way?
interpret: Why do you think John tells us that Siloam means Sent? How does that detail connect the healing to Jesus?
What does Jesus mean in verse 41 when he says that claiming to see leaves a person's guilt in place?
Why is it significant that Jesus finds the man after he has been thrown out, rather than before?
apply: The man could say only what he knew: “I was blind, but now I see!” How might your own honest testimony matter even when you can't answer every question?
His parents were afraid to speak because of what it might cost them. Where does fear of losing your place keep you quiet?
Where are you most tempted to say ‘we know’ in a way that keeps you from seeing what Jesus is doing?
